The recent sequence shows that I've successfully added the frontend app.js, updated task statuses, synchronized dependencies, and wrote a comprehensive test suite for the studio backend. I then ran the studio tests, encountered a validation error regarding the prompts file, edited `project.py` to handle missing prompts files more gracefully, and re‑ran the tests. After the fix, all studio tests passed (17 passed). 

Now that the studio component is stable, I should verify that the rest of the repository's test suite also passes, especially since new code was added (the frontend JS file and the test file). The repository includes a fairly extensive test collection covering many parts of the project: CLI, configuration, conversion, formatting, integration, loader, runner, tokenizer, etc. Running the full suite will ensure that my recent changes didn't break anything elsewhere.

However, there are some tests marked as `integration`, `slow`, or `tokenizer_smoke`. Those can take a long time or require external resources, and the prompt likely expects a quicker verification. The typical pattern in this workflow is to run the test suite while excluding those heavy markers, using `pytest -m "not integration and not slow and not tokenizer_smoke"`. This will run all fast unit tests and give a quick sanity check.

After confirming that the tests pass, I should also run the linter (ruff) on the newly added/modified source files to ensure code style compliance. The relevant paths are the studio package (`src/teich/studio`) and the CLI entry point (`src/teich/cli.py`). Running `ruff check` on those directories will surface any style violations introduced by the recent edits.

I want to capture concise output, so I’ll pipe both commands through `tail` to show only the final few lines, which typically contain the summary of passed tests and any linter warnings/errors. Combining both commands in a single Bash tool call makes the workflow efficient.

Thus, the next logical step is to execute a Bash command that runs the filtered pytest suite and then runs ruff on the target files, capturing the tail of each output. This aligns with the pattern used earlier (running pytest with `tail -3` and ruff with `tail -5`). I will construct the command accordingly and invoke the Bash tool.

arguments.command: uv run pytest -q -m "not integration and not slow and not tokenizer_smoke" 2>&1 | tail -3 && uv run ruff check src/teich/studio src/teich/cli.py 2>&1 | tail -5
